item.title: Optimizing tomato plant growth with microbes
item.description: Plants are home to a diverse array of microorganisms that support their growth and help them adapt to environmental stress—of which there has been an abundance lately. High temperatures and drought caused by human-induced climate change have led to reduced crop yields and the use of biofertilizers such as rhizosphere microorganisms, which help plants absorb nutrients and increase their resistance to disease and stress. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Rural towns finding the right medicine to end doctor drought
item.description: Nearly a third of medical graduates are taking up general practice, and health experts say it is an opportunity to rebuild rural practices from the ground up. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.description: In the village forests of Uttarakhand, in the Himalayan region of northern India, a tree can be charred at its base while maintaining a green canopy at its peak. item.title: Indigenous peoples near Congo parks propose diverse solutions for the future of conservation
item.description: GOMA, Democratic Republic of Congo — High above the lush forests of protected areas in the Congo Basin in eastern Congo, the calls of endemic birds and monkeys echo through the trees. Beneath the canopy, the Maiko, Salonga, Kahuzi-Biega, and Virunga National Parks sprawl across millions of hectares. For millennia, long before these protected areas […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.description: Mongabay staff writer Aimee Gabay joins the Newscast this week to discuss her reporting trip to the Peruvian Amazon, where she spoke with the Indigenous Matsés community. She made the trip initially to examine environmental threats to Matsés territory. Instead, she found them suffering from an epidemic of malaria and hepatitis B, which they have […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: Singkil peat swamp: The embattled orangutan capital of the world
item.description: Deep within Indonesia’s Leuser Ecosystem, one of the most important peat swamp forests left on Earth is being cleared, drained, and burned. The Singkil peat swamp is the largest of three remaining coastal peat swamp forests on Sumatra’s west coast, alongside Kluet and Tripa. Together, these extraordinary peatlands form what’s been called “the orangutan capital […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: Quebec wildfire smoke left forest moths with deformed wings, research finds
item.description: Over the course of the summer of 2023, Quebec experienced its worst wildfire season on record. By its end, some 4.5 million hectares (11.1 million acres) of the province's boreal forest had burned. While the effects of the toxic smoke on humans have been thoroughly studied, our knowledge of the impact on local fauna—including insects—is lacking. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Riverside families in the Amazon change meals as mercury poisons staple fish
item.description: A database built by Mongabay Latam, based on the analysis of scientific studies that gathered more than 7,000 samples from humans and 5,900 from fish, identified the areas most affected by mercury contamination in the Madeira River, one of the main tributaries of the Amazon. Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: In Peru, mercury leaves a toxic footprint on those who depend on a river
item.description: Mongabay reviewed nearly three decades of scientific research on the impact of heavy metals and traveled to several Amazonian communities to track the course of mercury contamination. Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: Indigenous territories maintain Amazon forest just as well as protected areas, study finds
item.description: A new study has found that in Ecuador’s Amazon, Indigenous territories without formal conservation contracts maintained forest conditions just as well as formal protected areas. Ecuador has three different approaches to forest governance: Forests protected by government institutions, forests managed by local communities under formal conservation agreements and Indigenous territories without formal conservation agreements. To […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: Too hot to learn: How climate change hurts children's chances from birth
item.description: Children across Europe have returned to school after a summer of extreme heat. As the climate warms, one question is becoming harder to ignore: How can students learn when classrooms become dangerously hot? Fuente: Phys.org.

Nearly all of them exceed the limits considered safe by the World Health Organization. The stories reported by three journalistic teams […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: In Nepal, climate adaptation starts with what communities already know
item.description: The catastrophic flood along the Nepal–China border that killed more than 1,400 people and left nearly 6,000 people missing devastated communities and infrastructure and renewed questions about how Himalayan countries prepare for environmental hazards that can unfold rapidly and cross-national borders. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Climate change may erase 25 million hectares of kelp forests by 2050
item.description: Climate change is driving rapid declines in seaweed forests globally, outpacing restoration efforts and undermining seaweed restoration as a viable carbon dioxide removal strategy, according to an essay by Karen Filbee-Dexter at the University of Western Australia and colleagues, published Sept. 8 in the journal PLOS Biology. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US federal court says no constitutional right to clean water in Mississippi case
item.description: Appeals court dismisses lawsuit from Jackson residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their rights A US appellate court has decided that the federal constitution does not guarantee a right to clean water. That legal opinion came in the form of a decision on Friday from the fifth circuit court of appeals to uphold a lower court’s dismissal of a 2022 lawsuit from several Jackson, Mississippi, residents claiming that tainted drinking water violated their constitutional rights. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: She bought a Maine island to stop clear-cutting; 90 years after Audubon opened its first camp there
item.description: Hog Island Audubon Camp marks an impressive ninety years of promoting environmental education and research. Located in Maine, this island was rescued from deforestation by environmentalists Millicent Todd Bingham and Mabel Loomis Todd. The camp is also the birthplace of Project Puffin, which successfully revitalized seabird numbers. Today, it remains a vital training ground for future scientists, educators, and artists, with its influence extending to bird conservation throughout North America. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Carbon credit financing emerges as Africa’s biggest bet for expanding clean cooking
item.description: NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Carbon credit financing is helping to drive Africa’s clean cooking transition by making cleaner stoves affordable for millions of low-income households. As governments introduce new policies, securing $900 million in fresh financing commitments, companies such as Kenya’s BURN are using carbon credits to subsidize electric and efficient biomass cookstoves across the […] Fuente: Mongabay.

item.title: Plants' response to rising CO₂ could put the brakes on dryland expansion
item.description: Drylands are defined as regions where rainfall is low relative to the atmosphere's ability to draw water from soil and plants. Expanding boundaries of these regions are frequent concerns in climate change considerations. While they can support large populations and ecosystems, dryland expansion can worsen water scarcity, land degradation and desertification. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: 5.3-magnitude quake hits Tibet as region reels from deadly flash floods
item.description: A magnitude 5.3 earthquake struck Tibet recently, following another tremor last week. Devastating flash floods hit the Tibet-Nepal border on August 26, causing widespread destruction. The disaster has raised concerns over the fragile Qinghai-Tibet Plateau environment. Rising temperatures and glacier melt are cited as contributing factors to the floods. Nepal's death toll from the floods has risen to 1,357 people. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: Yashasvi Vasistha

item.title: Heat waves inhibit antibiotic resistance in soils, but at a price
item.description: Extreme heat waves disrupt life in soil. Soil bacteria that produce and resist antibiotics switch into survival mode, temporarily reducing the number of resistance genes. At the same time, heat and drought are causing significant damage to soils and ecosystems, especially in cold, wet regions such as the Netherlands. This is evident from a large-scale European study by soil ecologist Franciska de Vries (University of Amsterdam) and colleagues. The findings are published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hurricane Lowell brings threat of floods, mudslides and tornadoes to Hawaii
item.description: Center of storm passed west of the islands and was moving away but flooding and mudslides will continue to be a risk Damaging winds and heavy rains from Hurricane Lowell pelted Hawaii ’s western islands on Tuesday, knocking out power and bringing the threat of flash floods and mudslides. Fierce winds downed trees and caused widespread power outages on the island of Kauai, home to 73,000 residents. The Kauai island utility cooperative reported that nearly all of its members were without power early Tuesday. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.description: Scientists recently described a new species of a tiny brown frog found in the Amazonian floodplain forests of Ecuador and northwestern Brazil. item.title: Current events: Scientists keep close eye on Atlantic Ocean changes
item.description: The year is 2060. London shudders through months of Nordic winter freezes. Across northern Europe, oak and beech forests wither under severe frost and drought, while cereal yields collapse from temperatures plunging as low as 27 degrees Fahrenheit below today's averages. In U.S. coastal cities such as Miami and Charleston, South Carolina, sea levels have risen three feet (about 0.9 meters), with routine tidal flooding washing away streets. Meanwhile, in the North Atlantic, deep-sea nutrients remain trapped on the ocean floor, starving plankton blooms and triggering a cascade of die-offs from… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Marine heat waves boost coastal CO₂ uptake by 11%, analysis finds
item.description: Marine heat waves are a consequence of climate change and are increasingly altering marine and coastal regions worldwide. An international study led by the Helmholtz-Zentrum Hereon now shows that many coastal seas absorb more CO₂ from the atmosphere during these extreme events than under normal conditions. The effect is particularly pronounced in polar and subpolar shelf seas of the Northern Hemisphere, where sea ice is declining as temperatures rise. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Panama City school left empty for years is getting a second life
item.description: The former Panama City Grammar School will undergo redevelopment into apartments and townhomes. City officials have cleared financial hurdles, waiving fines and providing a grant for the project. Developer Zachary Seymour will purchase the property and begin necessary structural repairs. The agreement mandates completion of critical repairs within one year to preserve the historic structure. Local leaders emphasize saving heritage, especially after Hurricane Michael's significant damage. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Central Park se adapta al cambio climático mientras ayuda a mantener fresco Nueva York
item.description: Las temperaturas en el parque pueden ser hasta 5 grados más bajas que en las calles de Manhattan. Pero el cambio climático ya está afectando al pulmón de la ciudad: aguaceros más intensos, inundaciones, erosión y olas de calor amenazan sus famosos manzanos y cerezos. "Los parques urbanos son más que espacios recreativos: son infraestructuras verdes vitales", afirma la directora del parque, que apuesta por adaptar un paisaje del siglo XIX al siglo XXI sin perder su esencia. Fuente: Noticias ONU.

The expected completion of the project, including accompanying sidewalks, is slated for late 2026. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

Hawkes, an associate professor at the University of Exeter, is co-leading a new three-year project to investigate the lives of three of England’s most vulnerable shark species. “I like the porbeagle, which looks like a baby great white shark,” she says. “Surfers could see one and… Fuente: The Guardian - Environment.

item.title: England released beavers into a Dorset woodland in 2025; one year later, their dams had...
item.description: Beavers newly introduced in Dorset have remarkably transformed a woodland area into a flourishing wetland. Through their natural dam-building, these creatures have slowed down water movement, resulting in the formation of deep pools. This ecological shift has rejuvenated the local fauna, reintroducing various native species to the Purbeck region. Additionally, the beaver dams serve to mitigate flooding on nearby roads during heavy rains, highlighting nature’s essential contribution to environmental resilience.
